item.content:encoded:
SonicWall SMA Zero-Days Exploited Before Disclosure to Gain Root Access — Must Read

A previously unknown threat actor, UTA0533, exploited two SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-days before disclosure to gain root access, install custom backdoors, and potentially capture credentials from affected appliances. SonicWall has released patches, and the flaws can be chained for unauthenticated access, command execution, and privilege escalation.

  • Volexity attributed the exploitation of SonicWall Secure Mobile Access 1000 series appliances to a previously undocumented threat actor tracked as UTA0533.
  • The attackers exploited CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 as zero-days before public disclosure, and SonicWall released patches for both vulnerabilities this week.
  • On one compromised appliance, the threat actor installed a setuid binary called ROOTRUN, a Python script called KNUCKLEBALL, the Suo5 HTTP proxy, and a Behinder-like Java web shell dubbed ORANGETAIL.
  • On a second compromised appliance, the attackers modified the NGINX Unit configuration and created files in the /var/tmp directory, including a script that launched tcpdump to inspect unencrypted LDAP traffic for usernames and passwords.
  • Volexity said UTA0533 obtained root-level access to the SonicWall appliances, but available evidence suggests the actor was less successful at moving laterally or gaining access to other systems.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-63030, CVE-2026-60137) WordPress Core Unauthenticated RCE via wp2shell — Must Read

WordPress released fixes for the wp2shell vulnerability chain, which enables unauthenticated remote code execution on default WordPress 6.9.0–6.9.4 and 7.0.0–7.0.1 sites, while 6.8.x sites still need patching for the SQL injection component. Administrators should verify updates to 6.8.6, 6.9.5, or 7.0.2 and review exposed sites for possible compromise.

  • wp2shell is an unauthenticated remote code execution chain in WordPress core that combines CVE-2026-63030, a REST API batch-route confusion issue, with CVE-2026-60137, a SQL injection in the author__not_in parameter of WP_Query.
  • The full remote code execution chain affects WordPress core versions 6.9.0 through 6.9.4 and 7.0.0 through 7.0.1, while WordPress 6.8.0 through 6.8.5 carries only the SQL injection component.
  • WordPress released fixed versions 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 on July 17, 2026, and the 7.1 beta line is fixed in 7.1 beta2.
  • The article says defenders should verify that automatic updates completed, prioritize sites on 6.9.0 or later, restrict or block /wp-json/batch/v1 until patched, monitor logs, and review potentially affected sites for compromise.
  • CyCognito’s observed exposure was spread across sectors, led by Consumer Discretionary at 18.6%, Industrials at 15.8%, and Communication Services at 13.0%.

Critical NGINX Vulnerability Can Crash Workers and May Allow Remote Code Execution — Must Read

F5 patched a critical NGINX heap buffer overflow, CVE-2026-42533, that can let unauthenticated attackers crash worker processes and may enable remote code execution in certain configurations. Organizations should upgrade to nginx 1.30.4/1.31.3 or NGINX Plus 37.0.3.1 because temporary mitigations may not fully close the issue.

  • F5 patched CVE-2026-42533 on July 15 in nginx 1.30.4, nginx 1.31.3, and NGINX Plus 37.0.3.1.
  • The flaw can let a remote, unauthenticated attacker trigger a heap buffer overflow in the nginx worker process using crafted HTTP requests.
  • Triggering the vulnerability can crash or restart the worker process and may allow remote code execution where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed.
  • Exposure depends on configuration and involves a regex-based map whose output variable is referenced in a string expression after a capture from an earlier regex match.
  • F5’s temporary mitigation is to switch affected regex maps to named captures, but researcher Stan Shaw said upgrading is the only complete fix.

UAC-0145 Uses ClickFix CAPTCHAs to Infect Ukrainian Devices wih Malware — Must Read

CERT-UA says Russian Sandworm sub-cluster UAC-0145 is using fake ClickFix CAPTCHA pages on compromised websites to trick Ukrainian users into running PowerShell commands that install stealers, loaders, and backdoors. The group is also targeting Android devices with disguised APK backdoors that collect files, contacts, and live geolocation.

  • CERT-UA attributed the campaign to UAC-0145, a sub-cluster within Sandworm affiliated with Russia's GRU military intelligence agency.
  • The attackers used fake CAPTCHA checks on compromised websites to instruct Ukrainian targets to execute PowerShell commands that could download and save a VBS file such as GHETTOVIBE in the Startup autorun directory.
  • CERT-UA identified additional malware on infected endpoints, including the SCOUTCURL reconnaissance script, FLUIDLEECH and LOADLOOP loaders, and the FREAKYPOLL Python backdoor.
  • At least 10 websites were assessed to have been compromised between June and July 2026, with the attackers using Cloaking.House and a bespoke tool called SMARTAXE to selectively display CAPTCHA checks.
  • CERT-UA also found that the threat actor distributed Android APK files disguised as security tools via messaging apps, containing the COWARDDUCK backdoor that can collect contacts, certain files, and real-time geolocation.

SleeperGem: Compromised git_credential_manager, Dendreo, and fastlane RubyGems Drop a Persistent Backdoor — Must Read

Malicious versions of three RubyGems packages in the SleeperGem campaign acted as loaders that avoided CI, targeted developer machines, downloaded a backdoor from git.disroot.org, and installed persistence via systemd and cron. Anyone who installed the affected gem versions should treat the machine and accessible secrets as compromised, remove the dropped artifacts, and rotate credentials.

  • Between July 18 and July 19, 2026, malicious versions of the RubyGems packages git_credential_manager, Dendreo, and fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab were published to RubyGems.org in a coordinated supply chain attack named SleeperGem.
  • The malicious gems check for about thirty continuous integration environment variables and exit without running if they detect a build system, indicating that developer machines were the intended target.
  • The gems act as loaders that download deploy.sh and a native git-credential-manager binary from an attacker-controlled Forgejo host at git.disroot.org, with certificate verification disabled and a User-Agent of Git.
  • In version 2.8.3, the installer copies the downloaded binary to $HOME/.local/share/gcm/git-credential-manager, starts it as a background daemon, and installs persistence through both a systemd user service and a cron entry.
  • The article advises anyone who installed or required the affected gems on a developer machine to treat that machine and every reachable secret as compromised, remove the dropped artifacts and persistence, check for /usr/local/sbin/ping6, and rotate credentials.

Hackers abuse ViPNet software to target Russian govt agencies — Should Read

A threat actor dubbed HelloNet is abusing the local update mechanism of Russia’s ViPNet security software to sideload malware against Russian government and critical-sector organizations. Kaspersky says there is no evidence ViPNet’s update infrastructure was compromised, and attribution to a Chinese-speaking APT is low confidence.

  • An advanced threat actor dubbed HelloNet is abusing the update mechanism for the ViPNet private networking product suite to target Russian organizations, including government agencies.
  • Kaspersky says HelloNet has impacted organizations in Russia’s government, energy, transport, education, and logistics sectors.
  • Attackers placed a malicious wtsapi32.dll file named HelloInjector inside the local ViPNet Update System directory so it would be sideloaded at system startup by the legitimate itcsrvup64.exe process.
  • HelloInjector injects into svchost.exe and runs an embedded payload called HelloProxy in memory, which contacts a command-and-control server to receive additional modules.
  • Kaspersky has tentatively attributed the campaign to an unidentified Chinese-speaking APT group with low confidence and recommends monitoring ViPNet systems for traffic on ports 5003, 5060, and 443.

The Policy PDF That Hid Its Link From Every Scanner — Should Read

A phishing email that passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC used a mostly image-based PDF with hidden URI annotations to redirect finance leaders through a compromised WordPress site toward the Microsoft 365 admin portal. The key lesson is that authenticated email and clean static file scans do not prove safety when malicious links are embedded outside readable text.

  • A finance team at an insurance company received a “Revised Policy” email that passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft compauth checks.
  • The attached scanned PDF was judged clean by static scanners because it contained no JavaScript, forms, macros, or embedded executables and had very little extractable text.
  • Forensic extraction found seven URI annotations in the PDF, including one that redirected through a compromised WordPress site to the Microsoft 365 admin sign-in portal.
  • The only visible text-level warning sign was a phone number in the signature block that was one digit different from the sender organization’s real published line.
  • Themis flagged the message at 90% confidence using behavioral and contextual signals and quarantined it across four affected mailboxes before anyone clicked.
